one_liner: C/x86-64-asm X25519 and Ed25519 library; precomputed fixed-base tables give 2.8x faster Ed25519 keygen than OpenSSL 1.1.1.
what_it_does: Small C library for X25519 key exchange and Ed25519 sign/verify, with an x86-64 assembly field-arithmetic backend (GNU as or MASM) and a portable-C fallback. The API is its own set of C functions over raw byte buffers: ed25519_CreateKeyPair, ed25519_SignMessage, ed25519_VerifySignature (or two-phase ed25519_Verify_Init/ed25519_Verify_Check per public key), curve25519_dh_CalculatePublicKey[_fast] and curve25519_dh_CreateSharedKey; optional C++ wrapper classes are included. It bundles its own SHA-512 and is not an OpenSSL engine/provider or a TLS stack, so adopting it means replacing EVP_PKEY calls with direct calls.
how_it_is_fast: Fixed-base scalar multiplication uses what the author calls FOLDING, which is essentially a fixed-base comb (Lim-Lee style): the 256-bit scalar is cut into 8 limbs of 32 bits, and each bit-slice indexes a 256-entry hard-coded table (source/base_folding8.h) of precomputed sums of 2^(32i)*B, so a base-point multiply is 31 doublings plus 31 mixed additions in extended twisted-Edwards coordinates. Verification computes s*B - h*A jointly with the 8-fold base table plus a 16-entry 4-fold table built once per public key (ed25519_Verify_Init). Field multiply/square/add are hand-written x86-64 assembly on 4x64-bit limbs using plain MUL/ADC (no MULX/ADX/AVX). Variable-base X25519 (shared secret) is an ordinary Montgomery ladder and gets no comb speedup.
when_to_use: Ed25519 keygen- or signing-heavy services on x86-64: 74,822 TSC ticks per key pair vs 210,738 for OpenSSL 1.1.1, and 78,628 per 32-byte-message signature (roughly 2.7x after removing OpenSSL's in-loop key rebuild; estimate).
Verifying many signatures from the same few public keys: call ed25519_Verify_Init once per key and reuse the context (about 103-111K cycles per check on an i7-2670QM in the README tables).
Generating ephemeral X25519 key pairs, provided you call curve25519_dh_CalculatePublicKey_fast (Edwards comb, about 43-48K cycles on i7-2670QM), not the plain ladder function.
Embedding a dependency-free MIT C implementation where you control the build: about 16 C sources/headers plus 7 x86-64 asm files.
when_not_to_use: X25519 shared-secret (variable-base) throughput: its ladder took 270,930 TSC ticks; subtracting OpenSSL's in-loop key construction (~208,714) from OpenSSL's 442,750 suggests OpenSSL 1.1.1's derive alone was faster (rough estimate).

When you need cache-timing-safe code without extra setup: fixed-base multiplies index the ~24 KB table directly by secret scalar bits; protection depends on blinding, which the X25519 _fast path cannot take per call.

Consensus or interop code needing RFC 8032 strict verification: Verify_Check does not check S < L or validate the public-key point, and CreateSharedKey does not reject all-zero output from small-order peer keys.
aarch64, macOS or other non-x86-64 targets: only portable C (32-bit limbs; README says asm is about 3x faster than C on 64-bit) and the Makefiles reject anything but Linux, Cygwin and MinGW.
Anything needing a maintained or audited library: no commits since 2020-04-20, open issues unanswered, no audit documented, and its OpenSSL comparison predates OpenSSL 3.x.

integration.form: static lib (libcurve25519.a portable C, libcurve25519x64.a asm) or source-drop
integration.dependencies: none at runtime (bundled SHA-512); build runs a bundled custom tool that generates custom_blind.h; OpenSSL 1.1.0+ only for the comparison test
integration.min_toolchain: Plain C with stdint types; GNU as (x86-64) or MASM for the asm build; documented builds: gcc 4.5.3 (Cygwin-32), VS2010, mingw GNU as 2.25; Makefiles use gcc and uname -o
integration.platforms: x86-64 asm on Linux and Windows (no ADX/BMI2/AVX needed); portable C for 32-bit and other CPUs, big-endian via -DECP_CONFIG_BIG_ENDIAN; macOS not supported by the Makefiles (a user in issue #9 reports it works after header changes)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the code read keeps no mutable global state (read-only tables and a build-time blinder), and per-key verify/blinding contexts are caller-owned
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — outputs match OpenSSL byte-for-byte in the test, but it is a separate C API over raw 32/64-byte buffers, not an EVP/ENGINE/provider replacement and not usable inside libssl

gotchas: curve25519_dh_CalculatePublicKey and curve25519_dh_CreateSharedKey take a non-const secret key and clamp it in place (issue #2); the plain CalculatePublicKey is the slow ladder that lost to OpenSSL, while the _fast variant is the comb path.

Side-channel protection relies on blinding, not constant-time table access: pass a context from ed25519_Blinding_Init to CreateKeyPair/SignMessage to blind the scalar; with NULL, only a static build-time blinder randomizes the projective Z coordinate.

The repo ships a fixed source/custom_blind.h; the Makefile regenerates it with custom_tool on each build. Vendoring the .c files without that step ships a public blinder, and omitting custom_blind.c gives 'unresolved external symbol edp_custom_blinding' (issue #13). The tool's RNG reads /dev/urandom in text mode without checking the fread length (author agreed in issue #10).
ed25519_Verify_Init mallocs a context when passed NULL and returns NULL on failure; Verify_Check does not check for NULL, and you must call ed25519_Verify_Finish.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over EverCrypt/HACL* or AWS-LC only when Ed25519 keygen/sign speed on x86-64 matters more than assurance and you want a tiny MIT C drop-in outside any TLS stack; for X25519 shared secrets, EverCrypt's formally verified Vale code (about 114K cycles per scalar multiply on its own test machine) is the better pick, and AWS-LC or wolfSSL are the choice when you need a maintained full TLS library.
verified_claims_summary: In a June 2019 run of test/openssl_test.c (asm build, gcc -O2, OpenSSL 1.1.1, HP EliteBook 755 G5, Ubuntu 18.04.2, CPU model not given; minimum of 100 TSC reads), Ed25519 key-pair creation took 74,822 vs 210,738 TSC ticks (2.8x), the only like-for-like row. The 5.4x sign and 1.6x shared-key rows count OpenSSL's EVP_PKEY construction, which recomputes the public key, inside the timed loop, and the 0.66x public-key row timed the Montgomery-ladder function instead of the faster _fast comb path; the separate 5.3x-19.6x figures are against portable-C curve25519-donna on an i7-2670QM.
status_note: Abandoned (last commit 2020-04-20; a 2024 issue and a 2022 PR sit unanswered) but MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor; the OpenSSL comparison predates OpenSSL 3.x and no security audit is documented.
